Yellow-whiskered greenbul nestlings hatch after an incubation period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] when eggs are maintained at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other members of the Pycnonotidae family. Upon emergence from the calcareous egg, the altricial nestlings exhibit a remarkably modest body mass, with freshly hatched individuals weighing approximately 2.75 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.75 grams]. This initial wet weight is among the lower range recorded for passerines of comparable adult size and reflects the species’ strategy of investing in a relatively small clutch, which hatches asynchronously over a period of several days. The nest-dependent chick relies entirely on biparental provisioning during its first days of life, during which time the developing bird undergoes rapid feather growth and internal organ differentiation. Field observations suggest that parental feeding frequency increases steadily throughout the nestling period to meet the chick's growing metabolic demands for thermoregulation and feather development, with the brood rearing cycle forming a critical phase in the life history of this Afrotropical species.

As the pin-feathered chick progresses through its development within the nest, a major milestone occurs when the fledgling achieves its first flight. Under the ambient thermal conditions typical of the species’ active metabolic period, measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging occurs approximately 14 days after hatching [tx = approximately 14 days after hatching]. Field reports indicate a range from 13 to 15 days depending on local food availability and microclimatic conditions. Shortly after nest departure, the fledgling enters a critical stage of nutritional independence onset, during which it begins to capture its own invertebrate prey while still receiving occasional parental provisioning. The ability to achieve flight at this relatively early age is consistent with the species’ reliance on dense understory vegetation for cover, reducing predation risk during the vulnerable post-fledging dispersal phase. This developmental schedule represents a finely tuned trade-off between the benefits of early nest departure and the physiological demands of flight feather maturation.

Reproductive maturity is attained after a comparatively prolonged period of somatic growth and behavioral development in the Yellow-whiskered greenbul. Published accounts indicate that the age at puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal activity capable of producing viable gametes, occurs at 34.5 days after hatching [tp = 34.5 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This figure, derived from captive colony observations, suggests that the species reaches sexual maturity earlier than many other Afrotropical passerines of similar body size, potentially as an adaptation to high nest predation rates that favor early reproduction. The pre-reproductive juvenile undergoes a period of rapid mass increase during the subadult stage, building the necessary lipid stores and muscle mass to support the energetic demands of future breeding attempts. Once gonadal maturation is complete, the young bird becomes a reproductively viable organism capable of participating in the annual breeding cycle. However, despite this relatively early physiological readiness, actual reproductive activity may be deferred in wild populations due to social constraints such as territory acquisition and pair formation.

Adult body mass in this species exhibits a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism, with field surveys and museum specimen series consistently documenting size differences between the sexes. Sexual dimorphism in body mass is evident, with adult females reaching an asymptotic wet weight of 25.1 grams [Wwi = 25.1 grams], while their male counterparts achieve a slightly greater ultimate wet weight of 27.9 grams [Wwi = 27.9 grams]. This modest dimorphism, which places males at roughly eleven percent heavier than females, is thought to reflect sexual selection pressures related to male-male competition for territories and acoustic displays. In terms of reproductive output, females produce a clutch of 2 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 eggs per nesting attempt], and typically raise approximately 2.3 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2.3 clutches each year] in a single annual breeding season. This reproductive strategy is consistent with patterns observed in the closely related congener Eurillas virens, suggesting a conserved life-history syndrome within the genus. The allocation of just over two broods per season is likely constrained by the protracted nestling and post-fledging care period, during which both parents invest considerable effort in provisioning the demanding young.

Basal metabolic measurements obtained from respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive individuals provide insight into the species’ energetic profile. The maximum resting metabolic rate, recorded at 65 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 65 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], is typical for a passerine of this body size inhabiting tropical lowland forests. Longevity records from banding studies indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 9.4 years [am = approximately 9.4 years], with data collected at the same reference temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Furthermore, the age at first successful breeding event, defined as the time since birth at first brood, has been estimated at 1.3 years since birth at first brood [tR = 1.3 years since birth at first brood] under comparable thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This combination of early maturation and extended parental investment positions the Yellow-whiskered greenbul among the slower-paced members of the Pycnonotidae, with a life-history strategy that balances moderate annual fecundity against high adult survival probabilities typical of tropical forest passerines.
